\title{Toward WCET Analysis of an Industrial \ndt{} Scan Matcher:\\
Deterministic Cost Search and Cross-Language Validation}

\author{%
  \IEEEauthorblockN{Yuuki Takano}
  \IEEEauthorblockA{TIER IV, Inc.\\
  \todo{email / co-authors / affiliations}}
}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Iterative scan-matching kernels such as the Normal Distributions Transform (\ndt) sit on the
critical path of autonomous-vehicle localization, yet their execution time is strongly
data-dependent, which makes worst-case execution time (WCET) analysis with classical static
methods impractical. We present a hybrid WCET analysis of the align kernel of the Autoware
\ndt{} scan matcher (map construction, preprocessing, and ROS scheduling are out of scope),
built around a Rust port of the production C++ engine that is bit-exact on the tested domain.
We establish a parametric bound on the algorithmic \emph{work} and empirically characterize
the \emph{time per unit of work}; we do not claim a certified hard time bound on the
evaluated platform. Deterministic algorithmic
cost counters --- compiled to zero overhead when disabled --- serve both as machine-checked
evidence for a structural work bound and as a platform-independent fitness function for a
worst-input search; because the two implementations are bit-exact over the bounded-neighbor
input domain (a runtime-checked condition), a worst input found on the
instrumented Rust engine transfers verbatim to the uninstrumented C++ engine within that
domain, with equal work
certified per input by an iteration-count assertion; the same counter transfer is validated
on a bare-metal AArch64 target, exactly, on all \raspiTotal{} frozen fixtures.
The search saturates the
analytic kernel-evaluation bound ($P \cdot \maxnn \cdot (N_{\mathrm{iter}}{+}1)$) exactly,
and a
controlled sweep shows the bound is affine in the scan size $P$. A two-tier formulation
separates the engine-API worst case (unvalidated inputs) from the preprocessing-reachable one
($\legalWorstRatioRust\times$--$\legalWorstRatioCpp\times$ apart on measured fixtures),
quantifying the value of
validating input contracts at the component boundary, and a
57-minute real urban drive (\num{22416} aligns, \realOnMap{} of them exercising the map)
provides one-drive evidence consistent with the contracts and margins --- its per-input
certification also exposed, and led us to fix, two port-fidelity gaps invisible to synthetic
fixtures, leaving a characterized residual of \realDivergences{} frames
(\realOnMapDivPct\% of on-map aligns). Measurements show the Rust
port meets or beats the C++ engine's observed maximum on every fixture (max-latency ratios
\tailsRatioMin--\tailsRatioMax), while the C++ engine performs ${\approx}\allocPerPtPass$
heap allocations per point per derivative pass (\allocWorstPerAlign{} per align on the worst
fixture) against zero for Rust, verified by a counting allocator under a declared capacity
contract; a unit-cost regression ties median latency to the
counters with $R^2 \ge \regRsqRust$ on both engines.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
WCET, measurement-based timing analysis, extreme value theory, Rust, scan matching, NDT,
autonomous driving, localization
\end{IEEEkeywords}
